\chapter{Small, and the Words That Never Change}
\label{ch:mr-invariable-adjectives}
\hlchaptermodality{50}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can call a thing small or beautiful, and I can tell from an adjective's last letter whether it will take an ending at all.}

Complete MR-R50-small and put all three adjectives on khoolī, naming which one changed and why.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[lahān]{\mr{लहान} (lahān) — small}

\label{lesson:MR-C50-lahaan}



\begin{quote}
Last chapter gave you \textbf{\mr{मोठा}} and the two rules it obeys. This word is its opposite and it breaks one of them.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{moṭhaṁ ghar}, then \emph{mājhaṁ ghar moṭhaṁ āhe}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{लहान}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{लहान}} — \emph{lahān} — \textbf{small, little; young}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{लहान} \mr{घर} · \mr{लहान} \mr{खोली} · \mr{लहान} \mr{मित्र}} — \emph{lahān ghar · lahān khoolī · lahān mitra}
\end{quote}

Three genders, one form. \textbf{\mr{लहान}} does not end in \textbf{-\mr{आ}}, so it has nothing to change, and it stays exactly as it is in front of any noun at all. Compare it with \textbf{\mr{मोठा}}, which moved three ways one lesson ago, and the contrast tells you which kind of adjective you are holding.

It also does the work English splits between \emph{small} and \emph{young}: \textbf{\mr{लहान} \mr{भाऊ}} is a younger brother, not a short one. Marathi treats age and size as the same scale for people.

Its history is a good one. Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{लघु}} (\emph{laghu}) meant \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{light, slight, small}\textquotedblright{} — the same ancient word as Latin \emph{levis} and English \emph{light}. The Marathi form wore \textbf{\mr{लघु}} down to \textbf{\mr{लहान}} over two thousand years, and the meaning barely moved.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{lahān ghar}, \emph{lahān khoolī}, \emph{lahān mitra} — nothing moved
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{moṭhaṁ ghar}, \emph{moṭhī khoolī} — and hear that something did
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \textbf{\mr{म्हणणे}} and report that your room is small
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many forms does \textbf{\mr{लहान}} have? (\textbf{One}.) What does \textbf{\mr{लहान} \mr{भाऊ}} mean? (\textbf{A younger brother}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%B2\%E0\%A4\%B9\%E0\%A4\%BE\%E0\%A4\%A8}{Wiktionary: \mr{लहान}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[lahān · lahān · lahān]{The adjectives that never change}

\label{lesson:MR-C50-adj-invariable}



\begin{quote}
Two adjectives, two behaviours. That is not an accident about those two words.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: only the -\mr{आ} adjectives agree}]
Marathi's adjectives fall into two classes, and you can tell which class a word is in by looking at its last letter.

An adjective ending in \textbf{-\mr{आ}} agrees: \textbf{\mr{मोठा} · \mr{मोठी} · \mr{मोठं}}. An adjective ending in anything else does not agree at all, in any gender, ever: \textbf{\mr{लहान}} is \textbf{\mr{लहान}} in front of every noun in the language.

That second class is large, and most of it is words Marathi borrowed — from Sanskrit, from Persian, from Arabic. A borrowed word arrived without a Marathi ending to change, and it never grew one.

This is the mistake to watch for in yourself. Having met \textbf{\mr{मोठा}} first, the temptation is to say \emph{\mr{लहानी} \mr{खोली}} by analogy. It is wrong, and it is wrong in a way a listener notices immediately, because no Marathi speaker has ever heard that form. \textbf{Check the last letter before you reach for an ending.}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{lahān khoolī} — and add nothing
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{moṭhī khoolī} — and hear where the ending was earned
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \textbf{\mr{शिकणे}} and that you are learning with a friend
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What tells you whether an adjective will agree? (\textbf{Its last letter} — only \textbf{-\mr{आ}} agrees.) Where do most of the non-agreeing ones come from? (\textbf{Other languages} — Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[sundar]{\mr{सुंदर} (sundar) — beautiful}

\label{lesson:MR-C50-sundar}



\begin{quote}
You have one word that never agrees. Here is a second, and knowing the class means you already know how it behaves before you meet it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{सुंदर}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{सुंदर}} — \emph{sundar} — \textbf{beautiful, lovely}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{सुंदर} \mr{घर} · \mr{सुंदर} \mr{खोली}} — \emph{sundar ghar · sundar khoolī} — \textbf{a beautiful house · a beautiful room}
\end{quote}

No ending, in either gender, because \textbf{\mr{सुंदर}} does not end in \textbf{-\mr{आ}}. You could predict that from the last letter one lesson before meeting the word, which is the whole return on having a class rather than a list.

The word came into Marathi from Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{सुन्दर}} (\emph{sundara}) unchanged, and that is exactly why it does not bend: it arrived already finished. Sanskrit built it from \textbf{\mr{सु}-} (\emph{su-}), \textquotedblleft{}good, well\textquotedblright{} — the same prefix behind \textbf{\mr{सुद्धा}} — so \emph{beautiful} is, underneath, \emph{well-made}.

It is a wide word in use. Marathi says \textbf{\mr{सुंदर}} of a person, a room, a song and a day, where English would reach for \emph{beautiful}, \emph{lovely}, \emph{nice} and \emph{fine} in turn.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sundar khoolī}, \emph{sundar ghar}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mājhyākaḍe sundar ghar āhe} — I have a beautiful house
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \textbf{\mr{मिळणे}} and how it puts you in the dative
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why does \textbf{\mr{सुंदर}} not agree? (\textbf{It does not end in -\mr{आ}; it arrived from Sanskrit already finished}.) What does the \textbf{\mr{सु}-} in it mean? (\textbf{Good, well} — as in \textbf{\mr{सुद्धा}}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%B8\%E0\%A5\%81\%E0\%A4\%82\%E0\%A4\%A6\%E0\%A4\%B0}{Wiktionary: \mr{सुंदर}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[moṭhā · lahān · sundar]{The last letter decides}

\label{lesson:MR-R50-small}



\begin{quote}
Three adjectives are now yours. Sort them into two classes before you say anything with them.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{moṭhī khoolī}, \emph{lahān khoolī}, \emph{sundar khoolī}
  \item \emph{Say it:} which of the three moved, and why — \emph{\textbf{\mr{मोठा}}}, because it ends in \textbf{-\mr{आ}}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mājhyākaḍe lahān sundar ghar āhe}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{mitrāśī} and tell your friend the room is beautiful
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the one test that sorts every Marathi adjective into its class? (\textbf{Does it end in -\mr{आ}?}) Where do all three of them stand? (\textbf{Before the noun}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
